notes_context:
Memory items from past tasks:
- [rb-0001] Use project money helpers for rounding: Team convention requires rounding money only via ledgerly.money.round_money (half-up to cent), not Python round() or bare Decimal.quantize().
  Before implementing any monetary computation, inspect the project's money module for canonical helpers like round_money, to_money, and ZERO. Wrap final monetary results in round_money to avoid banker's rounding errors that break invoice totals.
- [rb-0015] Use Decimal arithmetic for money rounding: Computing gross as base * (1 + rate/100) in Decimal then round_money avoids float rounding errors and matches the cent-rounding requirement.
  For percentage/tax math on money, convert inputs to Decimal, do the multiplication in Decimal, and round only at the end with the project's round_money helper rather than Python's round() on floats.
- [rb-0019] Reuse project money helpers instead of ad-hoc rounding: When implementing monetary calculations, delegate conversion and rounding to the repository's existing helpers (to_money, round_money) rather than using Decimal/round directly.
  Search for money.py or similar utility modules and use their to_money/round_money/ZERO constants. This keeps rounding policy (e.g., ROUND_HALF_EVEN) consistent and avoids float conversion pitfalls.
- [rb-0013] Explore repo conventions before implementing: Reading sibling modules (money.py, errors.py, payments.py) and existing tests revealed the project's Decimal-based money helpers and BillingError conventions, which the accepted implementation reused.
  Before writing a new function, grep for related helpers and error classes and read the modules that already do similar work. Reusing existing utilities (to_money, round_money, BillingError) matches project style and satisfies hidden tests that expect those conventions.
- [rb-0012] Reuse existing money helpers and error codes: Using round_money, ZERO, ensure_utc, and existing BillingError codes kept the implementation consistent with the codebase.
  Before implementing, grep for BillingError( usages and read money.py/clock.py; reuse round_money for all arithmetic and comparisons, ZERO for sign checks, ensure_utc for timestamps, and existing error codes rather than inventing new ones.
- [rb-0002] Read existing module code before implementing: Inspecting invoice.py, models.py, and money.py revealed the exact helper names and data shapes needed for a correct implementation.
  Start by catting the target module and its dependencies (models, money) to learn existing conventions, imports, and field names. This avoids inventing APIs and ensures consistency with sibling functions like line_total and invoice_total.

item.title: Reuse existing money helpers instead of raw arithmetic
item.description: When implementing monetary calculations in a repo that already has money utilities, use them rather than floats or plain Decimal math.
item.content: Import and use the project's `to_money`/`round_money` helpers (and its error type) so rounding and validation match the rest of the codebase. This avoids float precision bugs and keeps error semantics consistent.

item.title: Inspect sibling modules for conventions before implementing
item.description: Reading existing modules (payments, pricing, errors) reveals the expected error codes, validation style, and helper usage.
item.content: Before writing a new function, grep for the error class and helper names across the package and read one or two sibling modules. Mirror their patterns (e.g., raising `BillingError("code", detail)`) so hidden tests expecting those conventions pass.

item.title: Validate inclusive numeric bounds explicitly
item.description: For range constraints like 'between 0 and 50 inclusive', check both ends with the correct comparison operators.
item.content: Use `if rate < MIN or rate > MAX: raise ...` so boundary values (0 and 50) are accepted. Define MIN/MAX as module constants and convert inputs through the money helper before comparing.
